enhanced_recipes.name: Simple & Moisturizing Hot Process Soap Recipe
ingredients: 6 tsp grapefruit essential oil (24 g / 0.85 oz)
enhanced_recipes.instructions: Make soap from scratch using this simple and moisturizing hot process soap recipe. Pre-measure all ingredients, prepare your workspace with safety gear, and carefully make the lye solution by mixing sodium hydroxide into water and cooling it to about 120°F. Melt the solid oils on low heat, then combine with liquid oils in the slow cooker, bringing the mixture to around 120°F. Carefully add the lye solution to the oils, blend until reaching a medium trace (pudding-like consistency). Cook on low for 30-60 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the soap resembles vaseline. Remove from heat, cool to just under 180°F, then stir in melted mango butter, essential oil, and yogurt. Pour into molds, let cool and harden for at least 12 hours, then cure for 4 weeks before use.
enhanced_recipes.benefits: Moisturizing, skin nourishment, mango butter, yogurt, coconut oil, olive oil, castor oil, grapefruit essential oil.

enhanced_recipes.name: Homemade Hot Process Soap Recipe
ingredients: Moisturizing (Olive and Coconut Oil), Basic Natural Soap
enhanced_recipes.instructions:
1. Measure out olive and coconut oil. Place coconut oil in the slow cooker and turn it on to melt.
2. Measure out water and lye by weight.
3. Once coconut oil is melted, add olive oil to the crockpot.
4. In a well-ventilated area, slowly add lye to the water while stirring (NEVER water to lye).
5. Once lye is completely dissolved, add the lye/water mixture to the melted oils in the crockpot, stirring slowly.
6. Use a stick blender to mix until it comes to "trace" (pudding-like consistency).
7. Place the lid on the crockpot and allow the mixture to cook on LOW for 50 minutes. Stir quickly if it tries to bubble over.
8. Test the soap for remaining lye (the "zap" test). If it zaps, cook longer.
9. Turn off the crockpot and allow to cool briefly before mixing in optional essential oils.
10. Pour the soap mixture into the mold, press into corners, and smooth the top.
11. Set aside for 12-24 hours to set completely.
12. Remove from mold, cut into bars, and allow to dry for another day or so to harden.
enhanced_recipes.benefits: Moisturizing (Olive and Coconut Oil), Basic Natural Soap

enhanced_recipes.name: Homemade Aloe Vera Soap Using the Hot Process Method
ingredients: Aloe Vera (moisturizing, soothing), Tea Tree, Eucalyptus, French Green Clay. Perfect for beginners.
225g rice bran oil (can sub with more olive oil)
200g filtered tap water (or 150g for a harder soap)
enhanced_recipes.instructions:
1. Melt the oils: Add cocoa butter, olive oil, rice bran oil, and coconut oil to a crock pot (HIGH for 5-10 mins) or heavy saucepan (VERY low heat, max 80°C/180°F).
2. Prepare Lye and Aloe: Prepare the lye solution (water + sodium hydroxide, with safety precautions). Prepare 50g of completely blended fresh aloe vera gel.
3. Mix: Blend the clay into the melted oils. Add the lye solution to the oils and stick blend until the batter starts to emulsify.
4. Add Aloe: Add the aloe vera gel and continue to blend until the mixture reaches a very thick consistency (trace).
5. Cook: Cover and cook on low-very low heat for 15-20 minutes until the soap darkens and appears vaseline-ey (gel phase). Test for full saponification with pH strips.
6. Add Essential Oils: Remove from heat, cool for 5-10 minutes (no hotter than 80°C/180°F), and stir in essential oils.
7. Mold and Cure: Spoon the soap into the mould, banging down regularly. Allow to cool and harden for 1-3 days. Remove, cut into bars, and cure/dry for 4 weeks before using.

enhanced_recipes.name: Basic Hot Process Soap Recipe
enhanced_recipes.instructions:
1. Weigh out your oils, butters, and waxes. Pour them into the crockpot to melt.
2. When the oils have melted, put on your safety gear. Measure out your water and lye in glass measuring cups. Pour the lye into the water slowly to avoid splashes, and mix with a silicone spatula. (Do this step in the sink.)
3. When the lye is dissolved, pour the lye water into the crockpot with the oils.
4. Use your stick blender to mix the oils and lye water until you reach trace (looks like pudding).
5. Put the lid on the crockpot. Your soap will cook on low for about 50 minutes. Don’t leave the pot unattended. To prevent an overflow, remove the lid and stir. Otherwise, no stirring is required.
6. After 50 minutes, remove the lid, stir, and check the ph. If you are at a 7, your soap is good to go.
7. Set aside for 24 hours.
8. Unmold, cut into bars, and it’s ready to use!

enhanced_recipes.name: Basic Slow Cooker Soap Recipe
ingredients: Simple, moisturizing, coconut oil, olive oil, essential oils (lavender and orange mentioned as examples).
enhanced_recipes.instructions:
1. Weigh and combine olive oil and melted coconut oil in a slow cooker. Heat on high, then reduce to low.
2. Measure lye and water separately.
3. In a well-ventilated area, slowly add lye to water (NEVER water to lye). Stir and let cool for approximately 10 minutes until clear.
4. When oils are 120-130°F, slowly stir in the lye/water mixture.
5. Use a stick blender to blend until opaque and starting to thicken (trace).
6. Cover and keep on low heat, checking every 15 minutes. It will be ready when the entire surface is bubbly and the sides have collapsed in (35-55 minutes).
7. Turn off heat, remove the inner bowl, and stir in essential oils if desired.
8. Spoon into prepared molds.
9. Pop out of molds after 24 hours. Can be used immediately, but setting for a few more days is preferred for longevity.

enhanced_recipes.name: Almond Meal Soap
ingredients: 1 tbl intense almond fragrance oil (Note: Synthetic additive)
enhanced_recipes.instructions:
1. Put on protective gear (goggles and gloves).
2. Weigh liquid oils (18oz olive oil, 1 oz castor oil) into the slow cooker.
3. Weigh lye (4.9 oz) and water (11 oz, with some ice cubes recommended).
4. Pour lye into water slowly and stir to dissolve. Set aside to cool.
5. Weigh and melt solid fats (8 oz coconut oil, 6 oz palm oil, 2 oz shea butter).
6. Pour melted solid fats into the liquid oils in the slow cooker and mix.
7. Pour lye water slowly and carefully into the oil while stirring.
8. Use a stick blender to stir until it reaches a thin pudding/gravy consistency ("trace").
9. Set the slow cooker to "low," put the lid on. Check after 15 minutes for separation and mix if needed.
10. Check again in 20-30 minutes. The mixture will start to turn translucent from the edges inward.
11. Stir the translucent mixture every 20-30 minutes. It will look like apple sauce. Mix in the floating glycerin layer.
12. After 1.5 - 2 hours of cooking and stirring, the mixture will have a Vaseline-like consistency and is neutral. Turn off the slow cooker.
13. Add 5-6 tbls of almond meal and 1 tbl of intense almond fragrance oil. Mix well.
14. Scoop the soap into the mold, banging the mold to remove air pockets. Work quickly.
15. Once cool and firm, remove from the mold and cut. The soap can be used immediately.
enhanced_recipes.benefits: Almond meal (exfoliating), Olive oil, Coconut oil, Palm oil, Shea butter, Castor oil (moisturizing/conditioning oils). Note: Contains "intense almond fragrance oil" which is a synthetic additive.

enhanced_recipes.name: Cold Process Soap - A Basic Recipe
ingredients: Up to 10g of essential oils of choice (optional)
enhanced_recipes.instructions:
1. Start by melting your coconut oil. You can do this in the microwave or in a pan.
2. Carefully measure the lye and water separately.
3. Pour the water into a bowl or large glass jar. With gloves and eye protection, slowly add the lye to the water. NEVER ADD THE WATER TO THE LYE (this is really important). Stir carefully with a spoon, making sure not to let the liquid come in contact with your body directly.
4. As you stir, this will create a cloudy white mixture that gets really hot. Let this mixture set for about 10 minutes to cool. It should become clear and not cloudy when it has cooled.
5. When you have your melted coconut oil, pour it into a bowl and add the olive oil.
6. Slowly pour in the water and lye mixture and stir.
7. Quickly rinse the container used for the water and lye mixture out in the sink. I rinse well and then re-rinse with white vinegar to make sure all Lye has been neutralized.
8. Use the metal or wooden spoon to stir the lye/water mixture into the oil mixture in.
9. Once it is evenly mixed, use the immersion blender to blend for about 4-5 minutes or until it is opaque and starting to thicken.
10. If you are going to use essential oils for scent, add them now.
11. Quickly and carefully spoon into moulds. Any container will work, but I like loaf tins lined with parchment paper. I have included instructions for making one out of a box lined with parchment paper.
12. Cover the moulds with parchment paper and set in a cool, dry place, away from kids and pets.
13. After 24 hours, using gloves remove the soap from the moulds and cut into bars.
14. Leave the bars somewhere to cure for about 4 weeks. You can test if they are done by sticking your tongue on them (yes this is really what you do) to see if the lye is still active. It will zing you like a battery if they aren’t ready.

v2_recipes.name: Carrot Cold Process Soap
v2_recipes.instructions:
SCULPTING TOOL PREP:* First, you need to create the tool for the carrot shape. Cut a piece of sturdy cardboard into a “T” shape. Then, draw a carrot shape and cut it out. Ours ended up being about 2.5″ long from the bottom of the carrot to the top. Keep in mind that the exact size and shape doesn’t really matter. You can make it larger or smaller if you like. The top sides of the piece of cardboard will rest on top of either side of the mold. This will help keep the tool level throughout the process. If you’d like, you can also include a “lip” on the side (as seen in this tutorial). Because the carrot shape is less complicated and doesn’t need to be as precise, we didn’t include it. Once you’re happy with the size and shape of the carrot, wrap it in clear packaging tape. This helps make it stronger and more “soap-proof” as it’s moved throughout the mold.

* MOLD & TOOL PREP:* Line the Tall Narrow Wood Loaf Mold with freezer paper with the shiny side up. For tips on how to line the mold, click here.

* FRAGRANCE PREP:* Measure 2 ounces of Avocado Fragrance Oil into a small glass container and set aside. Measure 0.6 ounces of 10X Orange Essential Oil into a separate small glass container and set aside.

* COLORANT PREP:* Disperse 1 teaspoon of the brown oxide into 1 tablespoon of sunflower or sweet almond oil (or any other liquid oil). Then disperse 1 teaspoon of Nuclear Orange Pigment into 1 tablespoon of lightweight liquid oil. Use a mini mixer to get rid of any clumps. Have 2 tablespoons of walnut shells and 2 teaspoons of orange peel powder nearby.

* SAFETY FIRST:* Suit up for safe handling practices. That means goggles, gloves, and long sleeves. Make sure kids, pets, other distractions, and tripping hazards are out of the house or don’t have access to your soaping space. Always soap in a well-ventilated area.

* Slowly and carefully add 5.6 ounces of lye to 13.2 ounces of distilled water and gently stir until the lye has fully dissolved and the liquid is clear. Set aside to cool. If you’d like a harder bar of soap that releases faster from the mold, you can add sodium lactate to the cooled lye water. Use 1 teaspoon of sodium lactate per pound of oils in the recipe. For this recipe, you’d add 2.5 teaspoons sodium lactate.

* Melt and combine 2 ounces of carrot seed oil, 1.2 ounces of castor oil, 2.4 ounces of deodorized cocoa butter, 10 ounces of coconut oil, 13.6 ounces of olive oil, and 10.8 ounces of palm oil (re to fully melt then mix your entire container of palm oil before portioning) into a large mixing bowl.

* Once the lye and water have cooled to about 130 degrees F, split off 10 ounces of the oil mixture into a separate container. Then, very carefully (with safety gear on), pour off 4.7 ounces of the lye solution into a separate container. Set these aside – they will be mixed together to form the carrot.

* Slowly add the large batch of lye solution to the large batch of oils and stick blend until thin trace.

* Add the 2 ounces of Avocado Fragrance Oil and use the stick blender to mix it in.

* Add all of the dispersed brown oxide and 2 tablespoons of walnut shells. Use a whisk to mix them in thoroughly.

* The soap should be a thin-medium trace. Give it a few pulses with the stick blender if it’s still quite thin. Pour all of the brown soap into the Tall Narrow Wood Loaf Mold. Tap the mold firmly on the counter to get rid of bubbles.

* Now, it’s time to wait for the soap to firm and harden. The soap should be firm enough to hold its shape but thin enough to be scraped out smoothly. It’s a little hard to know when you have that “perfect” texture. We tested every 3 minutes or so by scraping a small amount of the very top of the soap with the carrot tool. It’s better to start scraping out the extra soap sooner rather than later. If the soap is not thick enough to hold any shape, let it harden for a few more minutes. But, if the soap is too thick, there is no going back. For this recipe, we found waiting about 8-10 minutes was the perfect amount of time to start carving out the carrot. Your soap may require more or less time, so keep an eye on it.

* Once the soap is an appropriate texture, insert the cardboard carrot shape and begin pulling it through the mold. Place the extra soap into a separate mold to save it. The first few passes with the cardboard will be a little awkward and messy, but that’s okay!

* Continue sliding the tool through the mold. As you move the cardboard piece down the mold, lift it up and out and discard the excess soap. Continue to move the shaper down the length of the mold until you get about three-fourths of the way. Try your best to keep moving the carrot in the same spot over and over again, otherwise you’ll end up with a very wide carrot.

* Once you’re almost to the other end, move the shaper in the opposite direction. Keep moving the carrot back and forth until it’s no longer catching soap.

* Once you’re happy with the shape, it’s time to mix the remaining lye and oils. Pour the lye mixture into the oils and stick blend until you reach a thin trace.

* Add the 0.6 ounces of 10X Orange Essential Oil and mix in with the stick blender.

* Add 1.5 teaspoons of dispersed Nuclear Orange Pigment and 2 teaspoons orange peel powder. Use a whisk to mix in.

* Gently pour the orange soap into the negative space in the mold. Continue to pour until it’s level with the top of the brown soap on the sides.

* We had a little bit of orange soap leftover. We let it thicken slightly, and poured it down the middle of the orange layer to build it up in the center.

* Use a small spoon to smooth out the orange soap and create a rounded top. Don’t worry about it looking perfect. Set the soap aside while you prep the last batch.

v2_recipes.name: Rustic Clay Soap
v2_recipes.instructions:
Calculate your recipe for the amount of soap you’re making to get the finite amounts of the fats, lye, and water. Unsure about how to use SoapCalc? I made a video to walk you through it! The video tutorial for this soap also features a lot of details on how to calculate the soap and how to make it from start to finish.

Put on your safety gear; gloves + eye protection of course, and an apron is also a good idea.

Prepare your mould—I used the loaf mould my dad made me for this soap, but you could use a cavity mould if you prefer.

Melt your oils together in your soaping pot and let your oils cool to slightly warmer than room temperature. Mix up your lye water and let that cool to about room temperature (I always use ice for part of your water to speed up the cooling process).

Once the lye solution and the melted fats have cooled to slightly warmer than room temperature, you’re ready to get started!

Blend the kaolin clay into the fats, and stir the sodium lactate into the lye water. Gently pour the lye mixture to the melted fats. Bring the batter to a thin trace. Once you’ve reached a thin trace, pour about 1/4–1/3 of the batter into a second container/pot, and blend the French green clay into that part of the batter.

That’s it for the batter! Pour the kaolin clay part of the batter into the loaf mould, and then knock the mold on your countertop to even it out and work out some of the bubbles.

Gently spoon the green batter on top of the uncoloured batter, smooth, and sculpt the top as desired. Once you’ve sculpted the top (I did a bit of a mohawk with my spatula), leave it to saponify.

After about 36 hours the soap should be firm enough to slice (though depending on your mould you may want to freeze it first—I used a silicone mould and froze it to prevent denting, but I don’t think you’d need to if you used a brittle mold that you can deconstruct to remove the loaf). Unmould it, trim off any dangly bits, and slice away.

Leave the bars to age (aka dry) for 3–4 weeks before using. Enjoy!

v2_recipes.name: The Beginner's Guide to Making CP Soap
v2_recipes.instructions:
Follow these steps to make your lye solution:

Slowly add the lye to the water

1. Using your scale, take a heavy plastic, heat-resistant glass or stainless steel container and place it on the scale – thus giving you the weight of the container. (Use the same unit of measurement you used in the lye calculator – either ounces or grams)
2. Once you have the weight of the empty container, press the \"tare\" button on your scale to return it to zero. You are now ready to measure your distilled water.
3. SLOWLY pour the distilled water into the container on the scale until you reach your desired weight. Be accurate!
4. Remove your water container from the scale and return the scale to zero (usually by hitting the “tare” button again)
5. Place your sodium hydroxide container on the scale. Follow the same process you did for the water container, measuring the weight of the empty container first, then pressing \"tare\", to bring it back to zero.
6. Next, take your sodium hydroxide and SLOWLY pour it into the container on the scale (You are wearing your gloves, right?) until you reach your desired weight.
7. Next, in a well ventilated area, SLOWLY pour the sodium hydroxide into the water. NOTE: Never pour water into sodium hydroxide!
8. Use your spatula to make sure the solution is well mixed. Avoid breathing the fumes as much as possible.
9. The solution will heat up. Set aside and wait for it to cool to between 95°F and 105°F3.

While the lye solution is cooling you can prepare your other ingredients and materials.

Choose your fragrance (optional), color additives (optional) and/or any additives \*\*(link) that you will be incorporating. Get them out and set aside so they're ready.

During this time, also prepare your mold.

Next you need to combine your oils/fats in the soap pot. Depending on how many oils/fats you have, you may need to repeat these steps several times:

1. Place an appropriately sized container for the first oil/fat on the scale and weigh it. Press the \"tare\" button to return the scale to zero.
2. Slowly either scoop (for solid oils/fats) or pour your oil into the container to the desired weight.
3. Pour the measured oil/fat into your stainless steel soap pot
4. Repeat #1 - #3 for each oil/fat you have in your recipe.

If your recipe contains solid oils/fats, you will need to melt them. Place your pot on a heat source (either a stove or a hot plate) and turn it on to medium heat. Do not leave your pot unattended! You do not want to overheat or burn the oils, only gently melt them. Stirring gently usually helps to break up the big pieces of solid oils and speed along the process.

Once the oils mixture is melted, turn off your burner to allow the oils to cool down between 95°F and 105°F4.

While you are waiting for the oils and lye solution to cool, you can measure out your other ingredients. If you are not using fragrance, color or other additives, skip this step.

For each fragrance, color additive or other additive, place an appropriately sized container on the scale and weigh it. Press the \"tare\" button to return the scale to zero. Slowly pour/place your ingredient into the container until you reach the desired amount. Set aside.

NOTE: As a general rule of thumb, don't use more than about 0.6 ounces of fragrance per 1 pound of oil/fat in your recipe.

Use your digital thermometer to tell when your oil and lye solution have reached the desired temperature. Once they are ready, you can start the final phase (before the dishes, that is).

Make sure you have everything ready at your work station - your mold, oils, lye solution, and fragrance and/or other additives. Plug in your stick blender and make sure you have your safety equipment on (put it back on, you know you took it off when you were waiting for things to cool down).

Begin by pouring your lye solution slowly into your fats/oils and stirring with your whisk. Once all of the lye solution is in, scrape sides and stir with the spatula until everything is initially blended.

If you are using a stick blender, completely submerge it in the solution. If you used a big pot, you may have to tilt it to submerge the blender. Using short bursts, start to blend the solution, trying to get the edges and the bottom, completely mixing everything. Scrape down sides with the spatula to be sure no under mixed lye or oil remains.

SLOWLY pour the lye solution into the oils

Use a stick blender to mix the soap

If you're not using a stick blender, then just keep mixing and mixing by hand. It will work fine, but will take a while longer.

The solution will start to thicken as it saponifies (combines to become soap). Once it reaches \"trace\", you are ready to pour it into the soap mold. \"Trace\" is when the soap mixture is still thin enough to pour off a spoon, but thick enough to leave a \"trace\" on the top of the pot as it falls back in. It's about like cake batter.

Add any fragrance, color and/or other additives, using whisk or stick blender to incorporate fully.4

Trace

Pour the soap into your mold

Slowly pour the wet soap into the soap mold. Be sure to get all of the soap out of the pot, and get it into all of the corners of the mold. Once the pot is empty and your mold is filled, lightly tap the mold on the surface of your work station to make sure the soap is set and to release any trapped air. You can clean the edges of the soap mold if you wish, but it is not necessary.

Wrap or cover the mold with a heavy blanket or towel to contain the head and allow it to rest and cure for 12-24 hours. It will get quite warm and then cool down. That is the saponification process taking place. Once the soap is fully cooled, you can unmold it.

Depending on your oils and water content, the soap may be soft when unmolded. Allow soap to rest until it is hardened up a bit (1 - 3 days) and then cut it as desired. Set aside in a cool area with good circulation for 4 - 6 weeks until the bars are fully hard.

Congratulations! You just made your first batch of cold process soap!

== From 'Cold Process Soap Recipes' (intro & method chapter) ==
Welcome to the World of Natural Soap Making!
Dear soap making enthusiasts, Are you ready to embark on a delightful journey into the world of homemade soap?
Today, I'm thrilled to share with you a simple yet enjoyable soap making recipe. Using natural ingredients that you can easily find at home, this recipe is perfect for beginners and seasoned soap makers alike.
But that's not all! For those looking to expand their soap making horizons, I have a variety of natural soap recipes for you to explore.
From soothing lavender and vanilla to refreshing aloe vera and green tea, there's a recipe to suit every taste and preference.
By choosing natural ingredients, you're not only creating a healthy and safe soap for your skin but also supporting a more sustainable lifestyle. Say goodbye to harsh chemicals and hello to the richness of nature!
I'm excited to share these recipes with you and can't wait to hear about your soap making adventures. Thank you for joining me on this journey towards natural living. Here's to many more days filled with health, happiness, and beautifully crafted soaps!
Let's get started!
Useful Tips Choosing the Right Oils
One of the fundamental steps in soap making is choosing the right oils. This will determine the final texture, lather, and effects on your skin. Vegetable oils like olive oil, coconut oil, and cocoa butter are commonly preferred. For instance, olive oil softens the skin while coconut oil enhances lather. However, this is just the beginning, as soap making can also reflect your personal preferences.
Using Sodium Hydroxide Safely Sodium hydroxide is one of the critical components of soap making. When used in the right proportions, it reacts with oils to initiate the saponification process. However, caution must be exercised while using sodium hydroxide as it is a potent alkaline substance.
Safety measures should be taken, and proper procedures followed. Adding sodium hydroxide in the correct proportions ensures
the quality and desired consistency of the soap.
Customizing Your Soap One of the most enjoyable parts of soap making is the customization phase. Here, you can add the colors, scents, and even texture characteristics you desire to your soap. Using natural colorants can give your soap an eye- catching appearance, while essential oils can impart a unique fragrance. For example, adding lavender oil can give your soap a soothing effect. In this step, you can unleash your creativity and create a completely original soap.
Maturing and Cutting Your Soap After pouring the soap mixture into molds, it's time to wait. This waiting period allows the soap to mature and harden. It's typically left
to sit for a few days, during which time the soap reaches the desired consistency.
Afterward, it's removed from the molds and cut into the desired shape and size. This is when you first meet your soaps in their final form, witnessing the unique and personal texture of handmade soap.
Using Your Soaps Finally, your prepared soaps are ready for use! Handmade soaps differ from commercial ones because they are often made with natural ingredients, thus treating the skin more gently and without drying it out. Making your own soap is not just a fun hobby but also a fantastic way to make healthy and eco- friendly choices. By making your own soap, you can contribute to healthier skin and a healthier environment.
Mixing Oils In soap making, oils are typically mixed in specific ratios to achieve desired properties such as texture, lather, and skin benefits.
Commonly used vegetable oils include olive oil, coconut oil, and cocoa butter. For instance, olive oil softens the skin while coconut oil enhances lather. These oils are usually melted at temperatures around 40- 50°C to ensure proper blending.
Using Sodium Hydroxide Sodium hydroxide (caustic soda) is used to increase the alkalinity of the soap. Safety precautions must be taken when handling sodium hydroxide, including wearing protective gear such as gloves and goggles.
It's typically mixed with a specific amount of water to create an alkaline solution. This solution initiates the saponification process, where oils and sodium hydroxide react to
form soap molecules and glycerin. The mixing process usually occurs in a well- ventilated area.
Blending the Mixture The soap mixture is blended at temperatures within a certain range, typically around 35- 45°C. This temperature ensures thorough mixing of oils and the alkaline solution, initiating saponification. Maintaining this temperature range is crucial for the success of the soap-making process.
Using Silicone Molds Silicone molds are often preferred for pouring the soap mixture. Silicone molds allow for easy removal of soap bars and are available in various shapes and sizes. The soap mixture is poured into these molds at temperatures
around 30-35°C to facilitate proper solidification and shaping.
Curing the Soap Finally, the soap bars are left to cure in the molds for several days to harden. After curing, they are removed from the molds, cut into desired shapes and sizes, and allowed to further dry and harden. Heating the cutting tool with hot water can help achieve cleaner cuts.

== From 'Easy Soap Academy - 32 Recipes' (welcome, equipment, basic steps) ==
Welcome to Easy Soap Academy Cold Process Soap Recipe Book The following recipes provide a sampling of ingredients, techniques, and products. The initial recipes are simple and the later recipes introduce new ingredients and new techniques.  All of these recipes are well within the capabilities of new and inexperienced soap makers.
Whether you are brand new as a soap maker or an experienced soaper, we hope you find the recipes to be good starting or jumping off points. Practice and experimentation are a wonderful part of the art and craft of soap making.
Each recipe describes the benefits of key ingredients. Remember that you may not make any claims for soap except that it cleanses. The listing of benefits is for your education.
Before making any of the recipes in this e-book, be sure you understand lye safety, have the proper protective gear, utensils and equipment. Since most recipes use a common set of equipment and utensils, these are listed before the recipes begin.  Any specialized equipment or utensils will be noted on the recipe.  Many of the ingredients are readily available at your local markets, hardware stores or big box centers.  All of the ingredients, utensils and equipment can be ordered online.
To assist your learning, keep a Soap Notebook to record recipes, trials, learnings, cautions and any modifications you made to the original recipe.  Check the Soap Business Planner – In the Handmade Soap Revolution Area under the "Classroom" tab for forms and ideas.
Before starting to make any recipe, assemble your equipment, supplies and ingredients. You may want to keep your utensils and equipment is a bin for convenience.  Read through the recipe more than once to be sure you have everything you need and understand the techniques described.
Some recipes require advance preparation of ingredients. Block out at least an hour or two of uninterrupted time so you can complete the recipe. If you have questions check out the online video library and ask for help from the community.
We would love to see your products in the "Your Soap Photos" section in the community.
Soaps are often scented with either Essential Oils or Fragrance Oils.  To be sure you are using these potent ingredients safely consult the free site, www.eo.calc, for safe usage rates for essential oils and the International Fragrance Association (IFRA) guidelines for Fragrance Oils.
Often the vendor for Fragrance Oils will provide IFRA certificates. Stay within the safe usage rates.  Most soapers do not use more than 5% for either even if it is considered safe to do so.
The recipes in this book are written in both grams and ounces. We list the method used to calculate lye and the percent of super fat that we recommend. We list the recipe ingredients by percent for ease in scaling your recipe to suit your desired batch size.
The batch size we have chosen is for one of the loaf molds most widely available on the internet. The mold holds approximately 1190 grams or 42 ounces (2.6 pounds) of soap batter based on 835 grams or 29.45 ounces of oil and produces about 10 bars cut to be 2.5 cm or 1- inch thick.
The appendix describes how to calculate the volume of your mold and scale your recipe to fit your mold.
CONTENTS A note on Ingredients: Do not substitute one oil or butter for another with out recalculating the required lye amount.
A note about when soap is safe to use:  The vast majority of the saponification process, a chemical reaction whereby lye and oil combine to make soap, is complete within 24 – 48 hours.  The soap is safe to use at this point.  The drawback to using it at this point is that the bar is still 'soft' and will not last very long.  There is still extra moisture in the soap because we used more liquid than we needed to dissolve the lye. We set the soap aside to 'cure' or dry for 4 to 6 weeks to produce the best possible, long-lasting bar. The soap will continue to harden as water evaporates until there is no additional liquid left.

Basic Equipment and Utensils for Making Cold process Soap
- Digital scale – weigh in ounces and grams – able to tare or set to zero
- Safety goggles and gloves
- Face mask – N-95 or better
- Heat-resistant glass or Type 2 HDPE high density polyethylene or Type 5 polypropylene plastic containers
- Stainless steel or heat safe plastic mixing spoons. Do not use aluminum containers or utensils including aluminum foil. Aluminum reacts with lye to create potentially explosive hydrogen gas and the aluminum corrodes to the point of failure.
- Silicone spatulas or scrapers
- Immersion blender – two-piece stick blender preferred
- Soap mold (If using a wooden mold, line with parchment or freezer paper before starting to make soap.)
- Parchment paper or Freezer paper (if using a wooden mold)
- Thermometer (Digital preferred)
- Measuring cups and spoons - stainless steel or plastic (see above)
Basic steps in Cold Process Soap Making While each of the recipes in this book provide a detailed step-by-step guide, there are steps common to all recipes. The variation comes in choices of oils and butters, choices of liquids, choice of fragrance, and choices of colorants. These are the basic steps in cold process soap making.
1. Preparation:
- Ensure your equipment is clean and dry.
- Prepare mold.  If using a wooden mold, line with freezer or parchment paper.
- Cover your work area with newspaper or a protective surface.
- Put on safety goggles and gloves
2. Mix the lye solution:
- Wear a face mask and avoid inhaling the fumes from the lye solution.
- Weigh liquid into a heat-resistant container.
- Weigh Lye
- Add Lye to liquid and stir until combined
- Set the lye solution aside to cool to about 38-43°C (100-110°F).
3. Prepare the Essential Oil Fragrance Oil: blend with clay if using fragrance
- In glass or stainless-steel container add clay and Essential or Fragrance Oil.  Blend thoroughly This helps anchor the fragrance as well as avoid speckles in the color.
4. Prepare, combine and mix the oils thoroughly:
- Weigh and melt hard oils and butters
- Weigh Liquid Oils
- Combine Oils
- Add Dry ingredients
5. Combine lye solution and oils:
- When oils and lye are correct temperature combine and blend to light trace
6. Add essential oil and clay
- Hand whisk mixture to incorporate fragrance and blend color.
7. Pour batter into mold:
- Tap the mold gently on the counter to remove any air bubbles.
8. Insulate and cure:
- Cover the mold with a lid or cardboard and wrap it in a towel to insulate.
- Leave the soap undisturbed for 24-48 hours.
9. Unmold and cut:
- After 24-48 hours, unmold the soap. If it's still soft, let it sit for another day or two.
- Once firm, cut the soap into bars using a knife or soap cutter.
10. Dry (Cure):
- Place the bars on a drying rack in a well-ventilated area.
- Allow the soap to dry for 4-6 weeks, turning the bars occasionally to ensure even drying.
11. Storage:
- After drying, store your soap bars in a cool, dry place.
- Your homemade soap is now ready to use.

== From 'Easy Soap Academy - 32 Recipes' (appendix: mold capacity & recipe scaling) ==
How to calculate the capacity of your mold and adjust any recipe to fit It is easy to calculate the amount of soap batter that will fill a rectangular mold. You will need paper and pen, a ruler and a calculator.
The basic formula is length x width x depth = total volume.
Length: Using a tape measure or ruler measure the longest side of the mold in inches or centimeters.
Width: Measure the shorter side of the mold.
Depth: Measure the depth of the mold.
When we multiply L x H x D we get a cube. The resulting number is either cubic centimeters or cubic inches.
Using the metric system is easier math. No need to worry about converting centimeters to inches – forget the label and just treat the measurements as numbers.
For example: L = 30, W = 10 and D = 5 When we multiply these numbers: 30 x 10 x 5 = 1,500 As it happens, this tells us that the mold holds 1,500 grams without any conversion.
Remember, we are not converting between centimeters and inches so these numbers do not correspond to each other.
Measured in inches L = 30 x 10 x 5 = 1,500 We have to convert this number to ounces with one more calculation.
1500 x 0.544 = 816 ounces.
Most recipes are built on the total oils which are a portion of the total volume.  We will use 70% as the total amount of oils.
1500 x 0.70 = 1050 grams of oils 816 x 0.70 = 571.2 ounces of oils Now, we know both the total amount of batter and the total amount of oils needed  in the recipe to fill the mold.
Check out the video in the Classroom Section under "Soap Making Class", "Workshop Recordings".
Since these recipes are provided in Percentages of Oils and Butters, Super Fat and Total Oil Weight we can convert the oils in the recipe as given to the capacity of our mold Recipe for Oatmeal soap from book 835 grams 29.45 Ounces Recipe 1 converted to my mold size 1050 grams 37.04 0unces 50% Olive Oil 14.69 50% 525.0 18.52 24% Coconut Oil 7.06 24% 252.0 8.89 14% Shea Butter 4.14 14% 147.0 5.19 7% Kokum Butter 2.00 7% 73.5 2.59 5% Castor Oil 1.49 5% 52.5 1.85 This conversion calculation will work whether your mold is larger or smaller than the one referenced in the recipe The easiest way to accomplish these conversions is through an online utility like Soapcalc.net.
Here are the steps in Soapcalc.net The application has an online tutorial but I'll just hit the high points. Select Recipe calculator from the menu bar. Each of the options that you need to provide information either have a radio button where you make your choice or a green shaded field where you provide information.  In Option 1, Type of Lye select NaOH as the type of lye. In Option 2 Select the weight of oils unit of measurement: pounds, ounces, grams. The green field defaults to 1 pound, 16 ounces or 500 grams. This is where you enter the total oil weight for your mold.
In our example above that is 1050 grams or 37.03 ounces.
Option 3 is Water. In our recipes we give you that information Most of the recipes in this booklet are listed as Water Lye ratio. You enter 2:1.
Option 4. Enter Super Fat – most of the recipes use 5% Super Fat. Fragrance - You can leave this blank if you want.
Option 5. The left columns provide you information, we are going to skip this for now and move to the next column selection of Oils, Fats, and Waxes. Use the drop-down menu to select the oils in your recipe one at a time.  Then add them to your Recipe Oil List. You can enter either percent by selecting the radio button over % or enter the actual amount by selecting the radio button over the unit of measure.
When you have all oils butters and waxes entered with the associated percent or value, press Option 7 Calculate recipe. The resulting recipe is displayed on another browser tab.
